text_to_image: First-person perspective. The protagonist is holding a small mechanical toy in the open palm of one hand. Below the hand is a wooden table that fully covers the background. The toy is small enough to sit comfortably in the palm and is currently in its untransformed state. It is a compact, fluted teardrop pod-shaped object made of dark cast iron with polished copper inlays. The outer shell is completely closed and solid, with fine machined seam lines where the separate fitted panels meet, but no gears, springs or moving parts visible anywhere on its surface. The toy features a small ridged copper stud on the underside. Shot on a 50mm macro lens at f/2.8, soft diffused window light from the upper left, shallow depth of field. Natural colour, fine surface texture with faint fingerprints and micro-scratches on the metal.
image_to_video: First-person perspective, filmed in one continuous long take, strictly no cuts or camera transitions allowed. The camera remains steady and does not move. The toy stays in the protagonist's open palm for the entire shot and is never set down. The protagonist's thumb presses the ridged copper stud briefly and withdraws; this takes under a second and nothing else happens before it. The transformation then begins immediately and fills almost the whole of the remaining shot, unhurried and fully readable from start to finish, never skipping ahead to the finished form. It runs in two stages that never overlap. Stage one: The fluted teardrop shell splits longitudinally along its copper inlaid grooves and the two halves pivot outward to each side, revealing intricate brass pinions and spring-loaded brass leaf springs moving inside. Stage two: A hinged beak assembly and two jointed steel legs extend and lock into place one after another, never all at once. Each emerging part appears exactly once and only at its natural anatomical position; nothing is duplicated. Every part carries weight: it accelerates, slows as it reaches its limit, overshoots very slightly and settles back with a small click. Panels slide against each other with visible friction and part along the seam lines already machined into the closed shell. Strictly no parts appear or disappear out of nowhere; every piece was folded inside, and the shell panels stay visible as part of the finished creature. The mechanism is simple and shown clearly rather than elaborate and rushed. After transformation, the final mechanical great spotted woodpecker's size remains believable and perfectly consistent with what the original toy could realistically unfold into, with absolutely no magical volume expansion. Once fully assembled, the mechanical great spotted woodpecker performs one short clockwork motion that imitates its species: its spring-loaded copper beak strikes downward once against its own chest plate with a sharp metallic clack. It remains an obviously mechanical toy made of metal, glass and gears at every moment; no skin, feathers, fur, flesh or any organic texture ever appears, and it never turns into a living animal. This motion is brief and takes only about the last two seconds; the transformation itself fills most of the shot. Only in the final second does the finished mechanical great spotted woodpecker settle into a still pose in the same spot in the palm where the closed toy sat, the lighting unchanged from the first frame, and the shot holds completely steady with no further movement and nothing entering the frame, so the clip cuts back to its opening without a jolt when it loops. Audio: crisp mechanical clicks, servo whirs and ratcheting gears, ending with a soft metallic latch as the transformation completes. No music, no voice.

concept.signature_move: its hinged bronze jaws pivot open wide on their pin and snap shut with a heavy mechanical clack
